title: The Wardrobe of the reservoir
premise: Wendell Marchetti, a literary translator who has spent a decade letting his childhood language — his mother's dialect of the drowned village of Rescarola — slip away word by borrowed word, learns that the last house from that valley, before the reservoir swallowed it, is being auctioned. Inside it he finds his mother's unfinished translation notebook and a single sentence she never rendered into any other language. As auction day approaches, Wendell must recover the words he's lost to translate that sentence — which turns out to be her confession of why she left him behind — and in doing so discovers that identity is not what you keep but what you choose to carry across. The book ends at the reservoir's edge, where Wendell speaks the sentence aloud in Rescarolese for the first time in thirty years, buys nothing, and finally belongs to himself.
about_author: Ulyana Nakamura was born to an Italian-Ukrainian family in a town later flooded for hydroelectric power, and worked as a court interpreter before turning to fiction. She writes about languages that die slowly and the people who survive them.

chapters.title: The Borrowed Word
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. In his Lisbon apartment, translating a mediocre novel, he reaches for a Rescarolese word for 'the smell of rain on stone' and finds only Portuguese waiting. He notes the loss in a ledger he keeps of vanishing words. Emotional beat: quiet grief disguised as professional routine.

chapters.title: Auction Notice
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. A lawyer's letter arrives: Casa Marchetti, the last standing house of submerged Rescarola, goes to auction in six weeks. His cousin Teodora calls, furious that he might let strangers buy their past. Beat: dread sharpening into obligation; the past acquires a price tag.

chapters.title: The Ledger of Losses
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV, with flashbacks to his mother Lucia teaching him lullabies by the pre-flood shore. He rereads his ledger — 1,400 words gone — and realizes he can no longer pray in his mother tongue. Beat: the scale of erosion becomes undeniable.

chapters.title: Return to the Water
chapters.summary: Wendell travels north. From the dam road he looks down at the reservoir covering the village, finding the church tower's tip above water like a periscope. Teodora meets him, brittle and accusing. Beat: homecoming to a place that no longer exists.

chapters.title: Casa Marchetti
chapters.summary: Teodora's POV. She shows him through the shuttered house: dust sheets, his mother's sewing machine, a locked writing desk neither could open. Auctioneers have already tagged rooms. Beat: intimacy violated by inventory; grief with price stickers.

chapters.title: The Locked Desk
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. He forces the desk at night and finds Lucia's notebook — half a translation project, and one sentence written in Rescarolese she never translated, underlined twice. He cannot fully read it anymore. Beat: fascination and terror entwined.

chapters.title: What the Sentence Says
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. He deciphers fragments: something about a boat, a name that isn't his father's, the word for 'forgive.' He begins hunting speakers of Rescarolese, most dead or scattered. Beat: the mystery becomes personal and accusatory.

chapters.title: The Last Speakers
chapters.summary: Alternating Wendell/Teodora. They visit old neighbors resettled in the valley towns; one woman, Serafina, sings a fragment but refuses to discuss Lucia. Beat: hope raised and dashed; a community guarding its own wounds.

chapters.title: Serafina's Silence
chapters.summary: Serafina's POV. She remembers the summer of 1974, Lucia and the ferryman Bruno, and why she promised silence. She almost tells Wendell, then sends him away. Beat: withheld truth as an act of both cruelty and mercy.

chapters.title: Borrowed Words, Returned
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. Working with a dying linguist's field recordings of Rescarolese, he begins relearning vocabulary like a foreigner in his own childhood. Each recovered word costs him sleep. Beat: humbling labor; love rebuilt through study.

chapters.title: The Ferryman's Son
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. He tracks down Rui, Bruno's son, now a fisherman on the reservoir itself. Rui confirms Bruno and Lucia were lovers the year the valley flooded — and that Wendell may be Bruno's son. Beat: the ground of identity gives way.

chapters.title: Two Fathers
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV, fractured and drunk on doubt. He rereads the untranslated sentence, now understanding its shape: it is addressed to a child, explaining a choice made at the water's edge. Beat: rage at Lucia; the auction becomes unbearable.

chapters.title: Teodora's Version
chapters.summary: Teodora's POV. She reveals her own secret: Lucia stayed for Wendell, giving up Bruno and the evacuation money, and asked Teodora to burn the notebook after her death. Teodora couldn't. Beat: sisterhood, guilt, revision of the villain-mother.

chapters.title: The Auction Opens
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs converge. Bidders wander Casa Marchetti measuring rooms; a developer circles; Wendell watches strangers price his mother's life. Teodora demands he bid or walk away forever. Beat: rising pressure; the house as contested memory.

chapters.title: Serafina Speaks
chapters.summary: Serafina's POV. Hearing the auction will scatter everything, she breaks her promise and tells Wendell the full story: Lucia chose to stay pregnant and alone so Wendell would be born on Rescarolese soil, in the last legal year of the village. Beat: catharsis; the mother reframed as fierce, not faithless.

chapters.title: Translation at Midnight
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. Alone in the house the night before auction, he translates the sentence word by word with everything he has recovered. It reads: 'I stayed so your first word would belong to this place; forgive me that it must also be your last.' Beat: climax of understanding; tears without melodrama.

chapters.title: The Gavel
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. At auction he bids against the developer using money meant for his retirement, loses by a small margin — then the buyer, moved by Wendell's public reading of the sentence in Rescarolese, deeds him the writing desk and notebook instead. Beat: loss transmuted into inheritance.

chapters.title: What Belongs to Water
chapters.summary: Rui's POV. Rui takes Wendell out on the reservoir over the drowned village square. They lower flowers at the church tower. Rui acknowledges him as brother, tentatively. Beat: reconciliation without resolution; new kinship on old water.

chapters.title: The Ledger Reversed
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. He begins a second notebook: not words lost but words restored, teaching Rescarolese phrases to Serafina's granddaughter via recorded voice memos. The language will not survive him, but it will outlast the moment. Beat: purpose found in transmission rather than preservation.

chapters.title: Speaking It Aloud
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. On the anniversary of the flooding, villagers gather at the shore. Wendell reads Lucia's sentence aloud in full Rescarolese, then his own reply to her, composed in the same tongue. Old women weep; children ask what the words mean. Beat: emotional summit; public mourning becomes shared speech.

chapters.title: Almost Saying It No More
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. Back in Lisbon, he finishes translating the mediocre novel and slips three Rescarolese words into it deliberately, untranslatable, footnoted simply as 'untranslatable.' His editor objects; he holds firm. Beat: integration; art as the vessel of identity.

chapters.title: The Wardrobe of the Reservoir
chapters.summary: Final chapter, Wendell's POV. He installs Lucia's desk facing a window, hangs his coat in it like a wardrobe holding one garment of the past, and writes the first line of a novel about a drowned village — in Rescarolese first, then English. Beat: resolution; belonging chosen, carried, and begun again.
